notes.front: What does “compute” mean in the study guide's cloud terms?
notes.back: A machine's ability to process information, handling tasks such as storage, retrieval and analysis.
notes.explanation: It is the processing power that workloads use, whether on-premises or in the cloud.
notes.example: Like the engine in a car: whatever the journey, something has to do the work.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a workload, in cloud migration?
notes.back: A specific app, service or capability that can run in the cloud or on-premises.
notes.explanation: The study guide's migration choices, such as retiring or retaining, are all described as things done to a workload.
notes.example: Like one item of furniture in a house move: each piece is packed, left behind or thrown away on its own.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an application (app), in the study guide's terms?
notes.back: A computer program or software that helps users do something.
notes.explanation: The study guide's definition of a workload includes apps, so the two terms often appear together.
notes.example: Like a payroll program that pays staff, or a booking site that sells tickets.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is discovery and assessment in a migration project?
notes.back: The first phase, in which an organisation takes an inventory of its existing on-premises environment.
notes.explanation: Google's migration guide calls this the assess phase: understanding the app inventory and its dependencies.
notes.example: Like listing every item in the house, and what depends on what, before booking the removal van.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does it mean to retire a workload?
notes.back: To remove the workload from a platform altogether.
notes.explanation: Retiring is one of the choices made per workload during a migration, alongside keeping or moving it.
notes.example: Like throwing out an old sofa nobody uses instead of paying to move it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does it mean to retain a workload?
notes.back: To keep the workload intentionally on its current platform.
notes.explanation: The word “intentionally” matters: retaining is a decision, not something left behind by mistake.
notes.example: Like leaving the piano in the old house on purpose because the buyer wants it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a rehost migration (lift and shift)?
notes.back: Moving workloads to the target environment with minor or no changes, only the minimum needed for them to run there.
notes.explanation: The only changes made are those the workloads need in order to run in the new environment.
notes.example: Like moving house and putting every piece of furniture in the same room it was in before.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Rehost: lift and shift”
notes.evidence: In a rehost migration, you move workloads from a source environment to a target environment with minor or no modifications or refactoring. The modifications you apply to the workloads to migrate are only the minimum changes you need to make in order for the workloads to operate in the target environment.

notes.front: What is a replatform migration?
notes.back: Lifting existing workloads and then optimising them for the new cloud environment.
notes.explanation: The optimising step after the lift is what separates it from a plain rehost.
notes.example: Like moving house and then swapping the old boiler for one that suits the new home.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Replatform: lift and optimize”
notes.evidence: In a replatform migration, you lift the existing workloads and then optimize them for the new cloud environment.

notes.front: What is a refactor migration?
notes.back: Modifying workloads to take advantage of cloud capabilities, not just to make them work in the new environment.
notes.explanation: Each workload can be improved for performance, features, cost and user experience.
notes.example: Like renovating the kitchen while you move, rather than only fitting the old units into the new house.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Refactor: move and improve”
notes.evidence: In a refactor migration, you modify the workloads to take advantage of cloud capabilities, and not just modify the workloads to make them work in the new environment. You can improve each workload for performance, features, cost, and user experience.

notes.front: What is a re-architect migration?
notes.back: A migration that changes how the workload's code functions, to take advantage of cloud properties such as scalability, security and agility.
notes.explanation: Google's example is splitting one large, monolithic workload into several independent microservices; it is more complex than refactoring, so it takes more time and effort.
notes.example: Like converting one large house into several flats that can each be let separately.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Re-architect: continue to modernize”
notes.evidence: Re-architect migrations are similar to refactor migrations. However, instead of restructuring how the workload code works, re-architect migrations change how that code functions. Those code changes optimize the workload and take advantage of cloud-optimized properties such as scalability, security, and agility.

notes.front: What is a rebuild migration (remove and replace)?
notes.back: Decommissioning an existing app and completely redesigning and rewriting it as a fully cloud-optimised app.
notes.explanation: It is also called rip and replace.
notes.example: Like demolishing an old house and building a new one on the plot.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Rebuild: remove and replace”
notes.evidence: In a rebuild migration, you decommission an existing app and completely redesign and rewrite it as a fully cloud-optimized app.

notes.front: What is a repurchase migration?
notes.back: Moving from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service equivalent.
notes.explanation: Google's example is moving from on-premises collaboration software and local storage to Google Workspace.
notes.example: Like selling your own washing machine and using a laundry service instead.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Repurchase”
notes.evidence: A repurchase migration is when you move from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service (SaaS) equivalent. For example, you can move from on-premises collaboration software and local storage to Google Workspace.

notes.front: What does reimagine mean, in the study guide's migration terms?
notes.back: Rethinking how an organisation uses technology to achieve its business goals.
notes.explanation: It is broader than moving any one workload: it questions the approach itself.
notes.example: Like a shop that, instead of moving its tills online, rethinks how customers buy from it at all.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a virtual machine (VM)?
notes.back: A software emulation of a physical computer that runs its own operating system on shared hardware.
notes.explanation: Several VMs can share one physical machine while each behaves like a separate computer.
notes.example: Like a flat in a block: your own front door and rooms, but the building's foundations are shared.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a container?
notes.back: A lightweight way of virtualising that packages code with its dependencies, so it runs the same in different environments.
notes.explanation: Packaging dependencies with the code is what gives the consistent behaviour across environments.
notes.example: Like a shipping container: whatever is inside, it fits the same cranes, ships and lorries everywhere.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are microservices?
notes.back: Structuring an app as a collection of small, autonomous services that communicate over a network, instead of one large monolithic block of code.
notes.explanation: The contrast is with one large, monolithic block of code.
notes.example: Like a food court of separate stalls instead of one restaurant kitchen doing everything.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is serverless computing, in the study guide's terms?
notes.back: An architectural pattern in which developers focus on their code's logic while the execution environment is abstracted away.
notes.explanation: Developers still run on servers; they just no longer see or manage them.
notes.example: Like taking a taxi: you choose where to go, and someone else owns, fuels and maintains the car.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are managed services?
notes.back: Cloud services in which the provider handles maintenance and operations, so users can focus entirely on the app.
notes.explanation: Maintenance and operations become the provider's job rather than the customer's.
notes.example: Like a serviced office: cleaning, repairs and heating are handled, and you just do your work.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Spot VM?
notes.back: A VM that uses Google Cloud's spare capacity at a much lower price, but which Google Cloud can reclaim (preempt) at any time.
notes.explanation: Google recommends them for cutting the cost of fault-tolerant workloads.
notes.example: Like a standby airline ticket: much cheaper, but you can be bumped when the seat is needed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs are VMs that use the spot provisioning model. This provisioning model lets you obtain resources at much lower prices compared to standard VMs. However, Compute Engine can preempt Spot VMs at any time to reclaim resources. Use Spot VMs to reduce costs for fault-tolerant workloads.

notes.front: What is Kubernetes?
notes.back: An open-source system that automates deploying, scaling and managing containerised apps.
notes.explanation: Its job is orchestration: deploying, scaling and managing many containers, not running a single one.
notes.example: Like a port's harbour master, deciding where each container goes and replacing any that fall overboard.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is autoscaling for a group of VM instances?
notes.back: Automatically adding VMs when load increases (scaling out) and deleting them when it falls (scaling in).
notes.explanation: Scaling out and scaling in are the two directions; the trigger is a change in load.
notes.example: Like a supermarket opening more tills when queues grow and closing them when it is quiet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, introduction
notes.evidence: Autoscaling works by adding more VMs to your MIG when there is more load (scaling out), and deleting VMs when the need for VMs is lowered (scaling in).

notes.front: What is load balancing?
notes.back: Spreading incoming network traffic across a group of backend servers so that no single server is overwhelmed.
notes.explanation: Sharing the traffic out is what keeps any one server from becoming the bottleneck.
notes.example: Like a head waiter seating arriving guests across all the tables, not just one section.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Cloud Load Balancing?
notes.back: Google Cloud's portfolio of application and network load balancers, built on the same technologies that power Google's own products.
notes.explanation: Maglev, Andromeda, Google Front Ends and Envoy are among the technologies it is built on.
notes.example: Like hiring the traffic-control system Google uses for its own services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Load Balancing overview”, introduction
notes.evidence: Google's Cloud Load Balancing is built on reliable, high-performing technologies such as Maglev, Andromeda, Google Front Ends, and Envoy—the same technologies that power Google's own products. Cloud Load Balancing offers a comprehensive portfolio of application and network load balancers.

notes.front: Why are rehost migrations the easiest and usually the quickest to perform?
notes.back: Teams keep using the same tools and skills, and workloads are moved with minimal refactoring.
notes.explanation: They also support ready-made software.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Rehost: lift and shift”
notes.evidence: Rehost migrations are the easiest to perform because your team can continue to use the same set of tools and skills that they were using before. These migrations also support ready-made software. Because you migrate existing workloads with minimal refactoring, rehost migrations tend to be the quickest, compared to refactor or rebuild migrations.

notes.front: What is the main drawback of a rehost migration?
notes.back: The moved workloads aren't optimised for the cloud, so they don't take full advantage of features such as horizontal scalability and managed services.
notes.explanation: Fine-grained pricing is another cloud feature they miss out on.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Rehost: lift and shift”
notes.evidence: However, after a rehost migration, the workloads that are running in the target environment aren't optimized for the cloud. These workloads don't take full advantage of cloud platform features, such as horizontal scalability, fine-grained pricing, and highly managed services.

notes.front: What does a replatform migration cost you compared with a rehost?
notes.back: More work: the new platform has a different underlying codebase, which needs several rounds of testing.
notes.explanation: The testing makes sure everything runs at its optimal level after the move.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Replatform: lift and optimize”
notes.evidence: However, replatform migrations take more work to accomplish than rehost migrations. The new cloud platform will have a different underlying codebase, which requires several rounds of testing to make sure that everything is running at its optimal level.

notes.front: When can the changes in a refactor migration be made?
notes.back: While the workloads are being migrated, or even before they are migrated.
notes.explanation: Teams with little migration experience may prefer to change workloads during the move.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Refactor: move and improve”
notes.evidence: You can modify the workloads while you're migrating them to the cloud, or even before migrating them. For example, if you don't have substantial experience with cloud migrations, you might prefer to modify the workloads while you're migrating.

notes.front: What are two costs of a refactor migration compared with a rehost?
notes.back: It takes longer, and it requires the team to learn new skills.
notes.explanation: The workloads must be refactored before the app can migrate, which adds time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Refactor: move and improve”
notes.evidence: However, refactor migrations take longer than rehost migrations because the workloads must be refactored in order for the app to migrate. A refactor migration also requires that you learn new skills.

notes.front: What is the trade-off of a repurchase migration?
notes.back: It may need far fewer resources than refactoring or rebuilding, but can cost a lot more and gives less granular control.
notes.explanation: The loss is the granular features of controlling your own cloud environments.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Repurchase”
notes.evidence: From a resources perspective, a repurchase migration might be a lot easier than refactoring, rebuilding, or re-architecting. However, a repurchase migration might be a lot more expensive and you might not get the granular features of controlling your own cloud environments.

notes.front: In Google's four migration phases, what happens in the assess phase?
notes.back: A thorough assessment and discovery of the existing environment: app inventory, dependencies, requirements, cost calculations and performance benchmarks.
notes.explanation: The other three phases are plan, deploy and optimise.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “The migration path”
notes.evidence: Assess. In this phase, you perform a thorough assessment and discovery of your existing environment in order to understand your app and environment inventory, identify app dependencies and requirements, perform total cost of ownership calculations, and establish app performance benchmarks.

notes.front: Which nickname does each source give replatform: the exam and study guides, or Google's migration documentation?
notes.back: Exam and study guides: “move and improve”. Migration documentation: “lift and optimize”, keeping “move and improve” for refactor.
notes.explanation: The documentation lists rehost as lift and shift, replatform as lift and optimize and refactor as move and improve.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Types of migrations”
notes.evidence: Rehost: lift and shift - Replatform: lift and optimize - Refactor: move and improve

notes.front: In the study guide's definitions, how does a rehosted workload differ from a replatformed one?
notes.back: Rehosted: moved to the cloud with nothing changed in its code or architecture. Replatformed: moved after changes to its code or architecture.
notes.explanation: The deciding question is whether the code or architecture is changed as part of the move.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do containers differ from virtual machines, according to Google Cloud?
notes.back: Containers virtualise at the operating-system level and share its kernel; VMs virtualise at the hardware level, each with its own guest operating system.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud also says containers are much more lightweight and use a fraction of the memory VMs require.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What are containers?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where can containers run, according to Google Cloud?
notes.back: Virtually anywhere: on different operating systems, on VMs or physical servers, on-premises, on a developer's machine or in the public cloud.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud presents this portability as greatly easing development and deployment.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What are containers?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a microservices architecture differ from a traditional monolithic application?
notes.back: A monolith is one tightly coupled unit; microservices split the app into small, independent, self-contained services.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud notes that a monolith's tight coupling can make it harder to scale, deploy and maintain as it grows.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is microservices architecture?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under a serverless model, who provisions and scales the infrastructure, and what do you pay for?
notes.back: The cloud provider provisions, manages and scales it; you pay only for the exact resources used.
notes.explanation: Serverless doesn't remove servers; it hides the routine infrastructure work from developers.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is serverless computing?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Compared with the on-demand price for standard VMs, how large can Spot VM discounts be?
notes.back: Up to 91%, for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs and Local SSDs.
notes.explanation: Spot VMs are excess capacity, so their availability varies with demand.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs are available at much lower prices—up to 91% discounts for many machine types, GPUs, TPUs, and Local SSDs—compared to the on-demand price for standard VMs.

notes.front: What happens to a Spot VM when Google Cloud preempts it?
notes.back: It is stopped by default, or deleted, depending on the termination action you set for it.
notes.explanation: Preemption can come at any time, for example when the resources are needed for other tasks.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: However, Compute Engine might preempt Spot VMs at any time, such as when it needs the resources for other tasks. At this uncertain preemption time, Compute Engine either stops (default) or deletes your Spot VMs depending on your specified termination action for each Spot VM.

notes.front: How do Spot VMs relate to the “preemptible VMs” named in the study guide?
notes.back: Spot VMs are the latest version of preemptible VMs.
notes.explanation: The study guide's cost section still speaks of preemptible virtual machines.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, introduction
notes.evidence: Spot VMs are the latest version of preemptible VMs.

notes.front: Are Spot VMs covered by a Service Level Agreement?
notes.back: No. Because of their limitations, such as preemption at any time, they are excluded from any Service Level Agreement.
notes.explanation: They also can't live-migrate or restart automatically after a host event.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “Limitations”
notes.evidence: Due to the preceding limitations, Spot VMs are not covered by any Service Level Agreement

notes.front: Where did Kubernetes come from?
notes.back: It was originally developed at Google and released as open source in 2014.
notes.explanation: It builds on Google's years of running containerised workloads, inspired by its internal system Borg.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Kubernetes?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Kubernetes automate for containerised apps, besides deployment?
notes.back: Among others: service discovery, load balancing, resource allocation, and health monitoring that self-heals by restarting or replicating containers.
notes.explanation: Self-healing means failed containers are replaced without someone stepping in.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Kubernetes?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What risk does load balancing reduce for applications?
notes.back: The risk that applications suffer performance issues, because the load is spread across multiple instances.
notes.explanation: Spreading user traffic is the load balancer's whole job.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Load Balancing overview”, introduction
notes.evidence: A load balancer distributes user traffic across multiple instances of your applications. By spreading the load, load balancing reduces the risk that your applications experience performance issues.

notes.front: What does a single anycast IP address give you in Cloud Load Balancing?
notes.back: One frontend for backends in regions worldwide, with cross-region load balancing and automatic failover to healthy backends.
notes.explanation: Traffic moves to failover backends if the primary backends become unhealthy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Load Balancing overview”, “Key features”
notes.evidence: With Cloud Load Balancing, a single anycast IP address is the frontend for all of your backend instances in regions around the world. It provides cross-region load balancing, including automatic multi-region failover, which moves traffic to failover backends if your primary backends become unhealthy.

notes.front: Does Cloud Load Balancing need pre-warming before a traffic spike?
notes.back: No. It can scale from zero to full traffic in a matter of seconds.
notes.explanation: It handles sudden spikes partly by diverting traffic to other regions that can take it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Load Balancing overview”, “Key features”
notes.evidence: Cloud Load Balancing can scale as your users and traffic grow, including easily handling huge, unexpected, and instantaneous spikes by diverting traffic to other regions in the world that can take traffic. Autoscaling does not require pre-warming: you can scale from zero to full traffic in a matter of seconds.

notes.front: During a migration review, a firm finds an old reporting tool that nobody has opened in two years. It decides to switch it off rather than move it. What is this?
notes.back: A) Retiring the workload
notes.choices:
A) Retiring the workload
B) Rehosting the workload
C) Retaining the workload
D) Replatforming the workload
notes.choicesExplained: C) Retaining would keep it running where it is. B) Rehosting would move it unchanged. D) Replatforming would move and optimise it; the firm is doing neither.
notes.explanation: Removing a workload from a platform altogether is retiring it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hospital decides to keep a specialist imaging system in its own data centre on purpose, because the vendor does not support cloud hosting. What is this?
notes.back: A) Retaining the workload
notes.choices:
A) Retaining the workload
B) Retiring the workload
C) Refactoring the workload
D) Rehosting the workload
notes.choicesExplained: B) Retiring would remove it altogether. C) Refactoring would change it for the cloud. D) Rehosting would move it to the cloud unchanged.
notes.explanation: Deliberately keeping a workload on its current platform is retaining it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A retailer must leave its data centre within three months. Its stock system works fine and there is little business need to change it. Which migration type fits best?
notes.back: C) Rehost (lift and shift)
notes.choices:
A) Rebuild
B) Re-architect
C) Rehost (lift and shift)
D) Refactor
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rebuilding means rewriting from scratch, the slowest route. B) Re-architecting is more complex than refactoring and takes more time. D) Refactoring takes longer than rehosting because the code must change first.
notes.explanation: Rehost suits a workload that can run as it is, when there is little business need for change, and it is the quickest type.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Rehost: lift and shift”
notes.evidence: A rehost migration is ideal when a workload can operate as-is in the target environment, or when there is little or no business need for change. This migration is the type that requires the least amount of time because the amount of refactoring is kept to a minimum.

notes.front: A company moves its web app to the cloud and, as part of the move, optimises it to use elastic computing and redundancy, testing it several times on the new platform. Which migration type is this?
notes.back: D) Replatform
notes.choices:
A) Retain
B) Retire
C) Repurchase
D) Replatform
notes.choicesExplained: A) Retaining would keep the app where it was. C) Repurchasing would replace it with a bought software-as-a-service product. B) Retiring would switch it off.
notes.explanation: Lifting workloads and then optimising them for the cloud's core competencies, such as elastic computing and redundancy, is replatforming.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Replatform: lift and optimize”
notes.evidence: A replatform migration is best for organizations that want to take advantage of all the core competencies of the cloud. These competencies include elastic computing, redundancy, improved performance, and security.

notes.front: A travel firm's booking engine needs a major update anyway, so it decides to change the code during migration to use cloud scalability and improve the user experience. Which migration type fits best?
notes.back: A) Refactor
notes.choices:
A) Refactor
B) Retain
C) Rehost
D) Repurchase
notes.choicesExplained: C) Rehosting changes as little as possible. B) Retaining keeps the engine where it is. D) Repurchasing would buy a replacement product rather than improve the firm's own code.
notes.explanation: A major update needed alongside the migration is one of the documented reasons to choose refactoring.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Refactor: move and improve”
notes.evidence: Another reason to choose the refactor approach is when a major update to the workload is necessary in addition to the updates you need to make to migrate.

notes.front: A law firm runs its own email and file-sharing servers and wants to switch to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service suite instead. Which migration type is this?
notes.back: B) Repurchase
notes.choices:
A) Rehost
B) Repurchase
C) Refactor
D) Retain
notes.choicesExplained: A) Rehosting would move the firm's own servers' software to the cloud unchanged. C) Refactoring would modify the firm's own workloads. D) Retaining would keep the servers as they are.
notes.explanation: Replacing a purchased on-premises workload with a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service equivalent is repurchasing.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started”, “Repurchase”
notes.evidence: A repurchase migration is when you move from a purchased on-premises workload to a cloud-hosted software-as-a-service (SaaS) equivalent.

notes.front: Before deciding anything, a council's technology team lists every server and application it runs and records which ones depend on each other. Which migration term describes this work?
notes.back: A) Discovery and assessment
notes.choices:
A) Discovery and assessment
B) Rehost
C) Retire
D) Reimagine
notes.choicesExplained: D) Reimagining rethinks how technology serves business goals, not an inventory. B) Rehosting is moving workloads. C) Retiring is removing one; nothing has been decided yet.
notes.explanation: Taking an inventory of the existing environment is the discovery and assessment phase.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A development team's app works on laptops but fails on the test servers because of different library versions. They want it packaged with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere. What should they use?
notes.back: D) Containers
notes.choices:
A) A load balancer
B) A larger physical server
C) Spot VMs
D) Containers
notes.choicesExplained: B) More hardware doesn't fix mismatched libraries. C) Spot VMs are about cheaper, interruptible capacity. A) A load balancer spreads traffic; it doesn't package software.
notes.explanation: Containers package code with its dependencies so that it performs consistently across environments.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A film studio renders thousands of independent frames overnight. If some machines are stopped part-way, the job just slows down. It wants the lowest compute price. Which option fits best?
notes.back: A) Spot VMs
notes.choices:
A) Spot VMs
B) A single large on-premises server
C) Standard VMs at the on-demand price
D) Retaining the old render farm unchanged
notes.choicesExplained: C) Standard VMs cost the full price. B) One server would be slower and needs buying up front. D) Retaining the old farm ignores the goal of lowest price.
notes.explanation: Fault-tolerant batch work that can withstand preemption is the documented use for Spot VMs, which cost far less.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: If your workloads are fault-tolerant and can withstand possible VM preemption, Spot VMs can reduce your Compute Engine costs significantly. For example, batch processing jobs can run on Spot VMs.

notes.front: Which workload is the worst fit for Spot VMs?
notes.back: C) A payments database that must never be interrupted
notes.choices:
A) Rendering video frames that can be retried
B) Overnight batch analysis that can restart
C) A payments database that must never be interrupted
D) Test jobs that can be rerun
notes.choicesExplained: A) Frames can simply be retried if a VM is reclaimed. B) Batch work that can restart tolerates preemption. D) Rerunnable test jobs lose little if stopped.
notes.explanation: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, so work that can't tolerate interruption should not rely on them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Spot VMs”, “What are Spot VMs?”
notes.evidence: However, Compute Engine might preempt Spot VMs at any time, such as when it needs the resources for other tasks.

notes.front: A start-up's developers want to write code and deploy it without seeing, configuring or scaling any machines, and to pay only for what their code uses. Which approach fits best?
notes.back: C) Serverless computing
notes.choices:
A) Buying physical servers
B) Running their own virtual machines
C) Serverless computing
D) Retaining their laptops as servers
notes.choicesExplained: A) Physical servers must be bought and managed. B) Their own VMs still need configuring and scaling. D) Laptops are neither scalable nor managed.
notes.explanation: Serverless abstracts the execution environment away, with the provider scaling it and billing for resources used.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is serverless computing?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An airline's app is one large codebase, so a small change to seat selection means redeploying everything. It wants each feature to be a small service it can change on its own. Which architecture fits?
notes.back: B) Microservices
notes.choices:
A) A larger monolith
B) Microservices
C) Spot VMs
D) Rehosting unchanged
notes.choicesExplained: A) A bigger monolith makes the problem worse. C) Spot VMs are cheap capacity, not an architecture. D) Rehosting unchanged keeps the single codebase.
notes.explanation: Microservices structure an app as small, autonomous services that communicate over a network.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company runs hundreds of containers and wants a system to deploy them, scale them, and restart failed ones automatically. Which fits best?
notes.back: A) Kubernetes
notes.choices:
A) Kubernetes
B) A load balancer on its own
C) Discovery and assessment
D) Retiring the containers
notes.choicesExplained: B) A load balancer spreads traffic but does not deploy or restart containers. C) Discovery and assessment is a migration phase. D) Retiring removes workloads instead of running them.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes automates the deployment, scaling and management of containerised apps.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A ticket site's traffic jumps tenfold when concerts go on sale, then falls back. It wants VMs added automatically during the rush and removed afterwards to save money. What does it need?
notes.back: D) Autoscaling
notes.choices:
A) Retaining the workload
B) A repurchase migration
C) A single larger VM
D) Autoscaling
notes.choicesExplained: A) Retaining is a migration decision, not a way to handle load. B) Repurchasing replaces software with a bought service. C) One larger VM stays the same size, paid for even when quiet.
notes.explanation: Autoscaling adds VMs as load increases and deletes them as it falls, cutting costs when less is needed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Autoscaling groups of instances”, introduction
notes.evidence: Autoscaling helps your apps gracefully handle increases in traffic and reduce costs when the need for resources is lower.

notes.front: An online game's login servers keep crashing because most players are routed to the same server while others sit idle. What would fix this most directly?
notes.back: C) Load balancing
notes.choices:
A) Discovery and assessment
B) Spot VMs
C) Load balancing
D) Retiring the login service
notes.choicesExplained: A) An inventory doesn't change where traffic goes. B) Cheaper VMs don't spread the load. D) Retiring the login service would stop players logging in at all.
notes.explanation: Load balancing spreads incoming traffic across backend servers so that none is overwhelmed.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A small charity wants to run its donation app in the cloud but has no one to patch servers or handle backups. What kind of cloud service suits it?
notes.back: A) Managed services
notes.choices:
A) Managed services
B) Self-managed physical servers
C) Retaining its old server
D) Rebuilding its own data centre
notes.choicesExplained: B) Self-managed servers need exactly the staff it lacks. C) Retaining the old server keeps the patching burden. D) Building a data centre adds work instead of removing it.
notes.explanation: With managed services the provider handles maintenance and operations, so users can focus on the app.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Modernize Infrastructure and Applications with Google Cloud”, p. 8
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
